parts.label: (a)(i)
hints: Hint 1: Start by thinking where the fast-moving charged particles come from in an X-ray tube and what makes them gain a lot of kinetic energy.
Hint 2: Next think about what those high-energy particles crash into - what kind of target material is used and why it must be a metal.
Hint 3: Finally recall what happens to kinetic energy when a fast electron is suddenly stopped - how is energy conserved as electromagnetic radiation.
parts.proper_answer: Electrons are emitted and accelerated through a large p.d. to high energy. They strike a metal target. Rapid deceleration of the electrons in the target produces X-rays (bremsstrahlung).
walkthrough:
Step 1: **Getting high-energy electrons**
Think of an X-ray tube as an electron gun. A heated cathode releases electrons by thermionic emission. These electrons are then accelerated across a vacuum by a large applied p.d. between cathode and anode, so each electron gains kinetic energy $E = eV$.

Step 2: **Hitting the target**
The fast electrons collide with a metal target, usually tungsten, embedded in the anode. The target nuclei exert strong electrostatic forces on the passing electrons.

Step 3: **Turning kinetic energy into X-rays**
The electrons are rapidly decelerated by the target atoms. The lost kinetic energy is emitted as a photon of electromagnetic radiation in the X-ray range. This is bremsstrahlung or braking radiation, suitable for medical imaging.

parts.label: (a)(ii)
hints: Hint 1: Think about what a single X-ray picture shows compared to what a doctor needs to see inside the body in three dimensions.
parts.proper_answer: Images of the multiple sections are combined by computer to form a 3D image of the structure.
walkthrough:
Step 1: **Building a 3D view from slices**
A single X-ray is only a 2D shadow. In CT, the X-ray source and detector rotate around the body taking many thin slice images. A computer combines all these section images to reconstruct a detailed 3D view of internal structures.

parts.label: (b)(i)
hints: Hint 1: Look at Fig. 9.1 and trace the ray that reaches point P - which material does it pass through only, and over what total thickness.
Hint 2: Recall how transmitted intensity falls exponentially with thickness and apply it using the correct $\mu$ and $x$ for that path.
walkthrough:
Step 1: **Identify the path to P**
The ray reaching P at the bottom goes only through soft tissue. From Fig. 9.1 the thickness is $x = 5.6\text{ cm}$ and for soft tissue $\mu = 0.89\text{ cm}^{-1}$.

Step 2: **Apply exponential attenuation**
Transmitted intensity follows: $$I = I_0 \exp(-\mu x)$$ Substitute the values: $$I = I_0 \exp(-0.89 \times 5.6)$$ $$I = I_0 \exp(-4.984)$$ $$I \approx 6.8 \times 10^{-3} I_0$$ This is the detected intensity from point P.

parts.label: (b)(ii)
hints: Hint 1: Trace the ray that reaches point Q - it passes through two different materials in series, so find the thickness travelled in bone and the remaining thickness in soft tissue.
Hint 2: Remember that attenuation by successive layers multiplies, which means you add the $\mu x$ terms in the exponent before evaluating.
walkthrough:
Step 1: **Split the path to Q**
At the level of Q the beam passes through bone of thickness $x_{bone} = 2.4\text{ cm}$ with $\mu_{bone} = 3.4\text{ cm}^{-1}$, plus soft tissue for the rest of the total width. So $x_{tissue} = 5.6 - 2.4 = 3.2\text{ cm}$ with $\mu_{tissue} = 0.89\text{ cm}^{-1}$.

Step 2: **Combine two attenuations**
Each layer reduces the intensity in turn: $$I = I_0 \exp(-\mu_{bone}x_{bone}) \times \exp(-\mu_{tissue}x_{tissue})$$ $$I = I_0 \exp(-3.4 \times 2.4) \times \exp(-0.89 \times 3.2)$$ $$I = I_0 \exp(-8.16) \times \exp(-2.848) = I_0 \exp(-11.01)$$ $$I \approx 1.7 \times 10^{-5} I_0$$ Bone attenuates much more strongly, so the Q intensity is far smaller.

parts.label: (c)
hints: Hint 1: Compare the size of your two answers in (b) - think about what a big ratio between neighbouring intensities looks like on a detector.
parts.proper_answer: Yes, good contrast because there is a large difference - factor of about 400 - between the intensities from P and Q.
walkthrough:
Step 1: **Link intensity difference to contrast**
Contrast means a clear difference in blackening between adjacent areas. Here $I_P \approx 6.8 \times 10^{-3}I_0$ while $I_Q \approx 1.7 \times 10^{-5}I_0$, so $I_P$ is about 400 times larger than $I_Q$. This very large fractional difference gives sharp distinction between bone and soft tissue, so contrast is good.
